1. What Huayan actually claims

3120 words · vendored research asset
source →

The central insight

  • e Reddit post is basically onto something important:
Huayan is a Chinese Mahāyāna synthesis that combines Madhyamaka emptiness, Yogācāra analyses of mind, tathāgatagarbha/original enlightenment, and the Avataṃsaka Sūtra’s vision of universal interpenetration.
  • t Huayan does not merely place these systems beside one another. It reinterprets and hierarchically reorganizes them, claiming that each expresses a partial aspect of the truth while Huayan’s “perfect” or “round” teaching shows how all the aspects mutually entail one another. Chinese doctrinal classification, panjiao, allowed apparently conflicting teachings to be treated as progressively more comprehensive rather than simply mutually exclusive. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])
  • compact formula would be:
  • Madhyamaka: nothing has independent existence.
  • Yogācāra: the world we experience is inseparable from cognitive construction.
  • Tathāgatagarbha/Awakening of Faith: deluded and awakened experience are two aspects of one mind.
  • Avataṃsaka/Huayan: because everything is empty, relational and mind-involving, every phenomenon contains and determines every other phenomenon.
  • at last step is the distinctive Huayan move.

1. What Huayan actually claims

  • e most useful entry point is Chengguan’s four dharma-realms.

1. The realm of phenomena — shi fajie

  • is is ordinary reality: persons, sensations, mountains, thoughts, chairs, rituals, atoms and moments. They appear as separate, conditioned things.
  • ayan does not tell you to deny this level. A chair functions as a chair; suffering functions as suffering; ethical action has consequences.

2. The realm of principle — li fajie

  • i* means something like principle, pattern, nature or truth. In Huayan it usually refers to emptiness, suchness and the absence of independent self-nature.
  • ery phenomenon is li because no phenomenon possesses an isolated essence.

3. The non-obstruction of principle and phenomena — li-shi wu’ai

  • ptiness does not exist behind phenomena as a second world. It is precisely the way phenomena exist.
  • wave is nothing apart from water, but water never appears except in some particular configuration. Similarly:
  • phenomena are entirely emptiness;
  • emptiness is entirely expressed as phenomena;
  • nevertheless, the particular phenomenon and universal principle are not simply interchangeable concepts.

4. The non-obstruction of phenomenon and phenomenon — shi-shi wu’ai

  • is is the distinctly Huayan climax.
  • cause every phenomenon is empty and constituted through relations, each phenomenon is internally connected with every other phenomenon. Every individual thing both includes and is included by the totality without losing its particular identity. Chengguan argues that the non-obstruction of li and shi grounds this further non-obstruction among all individual shi. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])
  • is is the philosophical meaning of Indra’s net: every jewel reflects all the other jewels, including their reflections of every other reflection.
  • is not merely:
“Everything affects everything.”
  • is the stronger claim:
The identity of each thing is constituted by its place within the whole network, while the identity of the whole is constituted by every particular thing.
  • zang illustrates this with a rafter and a building. The building depends upon its rafters, but a piece of wood is identifiable as a “rafter” only because of its role in the building. Whole and part therefore determine one another. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])

2. Huayan and Madhyamaka

  • ayan accepts the basic Madhyamaka insight:
Whatever arises dependently is empty of intrinsic nature.
  • dhyamaka applies this without exception. Bodies, objects, selves, consciousness, causation, emptiness and even Buddhist doctrines lack independent svabhāva. Candrakīrti’s criticism of Yogācāra is precisely that showing the objects of consciousness to be conditioned is insufficient if consciousness itself is then retained as a metaphysical foundation. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][2])
  • dhyamaka is therefore usually understood as anti-foundational:
  • there is no final substance beneath appearances;
  • no independently real consciousness supports the world;
  • emptiness is not a hidden Absolute;
  • ultimate truth cannot be captured as an entity or theory.
  • s two truths distinguish ordinary, conventionally functioning reality from the insight that phenomena do not arise through intrinsic natures. Even this ultimate insight is not an independently existing object. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][2])

Huayan’s difference

  • ayan asks:
Once everything has been emptied of independent nature, what does the world look like positively?
  • s answer is not merely absence. Emptiness means unlimited relational openness.
  • thing without a sealed intrinsic essence can:
  • receive determination from everything else;
  • contribute to the determination of everything else;
  • contain the whole relational order from its own perspective;
  • manifest the same emptiness/suchness as every other thing.
  • Madhyamaka tends to use emptiness primarily to deconstruct reification, while Huayan uses emptiness to construct a vision of total interdependence and mutual inclusion.
  • is does not mean Nāgārjuna denied interdependence. Rather, Huayan develops its ontological and phenomenological implications much more positively and elaborately.
  • useful progression is:
Madhyamaka: no thing exists from itself.
Huayan: therefore every thing exists through all things.
  • e famous Mahāyāna formula is:
rūpaṃ śūnyatā śūnyataiva rūpam
“Form is emptiness; emptiness itself is form.”
  • ayan radicalizes it:
Every form is emptiness; therefore every form is open to and present within every other form.

3. Huayan and Yogācāra

  • e Reddit post oversimplifies Yogācāra when it says:
“Everything stems from the ālayavijñāna.”
  • at is one possible schematic summary, but it can make the ālayavijñāna sound like Brahman or a cosmic creator-consciousness. Classical Yogācāra usually presents it more carefully.

What ālayavijñāna does

  • e store or substratum consciousness explains:
  • continuity without an eternal self;
  • the preservation of karmic tendencies;
  • how earlier actions condition later experiences;
  • how a structured world appears through the maturation of karmic “seeds.”
  • was developed partly to resolve problems created by combining no-self with the momentariness of conditioned events. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][3])
  • is generally conditioned, karmically structured and capable of transformation. It is not straightforwardly an eternal pure consciousness.

The three natures

  • gācāra analyses experience through three natures:

Imagined nature — parikalpita

  • e falsely projected division into inherently existing subjects and objects:
“Here is a self-existing observer; over there is a self-existing world.”

Dependent nature — paratantra

  • e actual causal flow of experience arising from conditions, habits, karmic seeds and cognition.

Perfected nature — pariniṣpanna

  • e dependent flow as realized to be empty of the imagined subject-object duality.
  • e perfected nature is not necessarily a separate substance. It is commonly defined as the absence of the imagined nature within the dependent nature. Nevertheless, some Yogācāra interpretations give the nondual dependent flow a stronger foundational status than Madhyamaka permits. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][3])

Is Yogācāra idealism?

  • at remains debated.
  • me readings say Yogācāra teaches ontological idealism: only consciousness ultimately exists. Others read it as phenomenology or epistemic discipline:
Do not make claims about a mind-independent world because everything you know is presented within cognition.
  • en Vasubandhu’s arguments against external objects can be read either as denying them outright or as showing that their existence cannot be established through perception. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][3])
  • one should avoid saying that all Yogācāra simply teaches that a cosmic ālaya produces everything.

4. How Huayan transforms Yogācāra

  • ayan was deeply shaped by the earlier Chinese Dilun and Shelun traditions, which had already blended Yogācāra with tathāgatagarbha ideas. It was also formed partly in response to Xuanzang’s more systematic “new” Yogācāra or Faxiang school. Zhiyan and Fazang defended universal Buddha-nature and suchness against interpretations that separated pure awakening more sharply from the defiled store consciousness.
  • zang considered standard Madhyamaka and Yogācāra valuable but incomplete:
  • Madhyamaka correctly teaches universal emptiness.
  • Yogācāra correctly analyses consciousness and karmic continuity.
  • But ālayavijñāna cannot itself be ultimate because it contains defilements.
  • Tathāgatagarbha teachings better express purity and original awakening.
  • Huayan’s “round teaching” then integrates emptiness, purity, dependent arising and phenomenal multiplicity. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])
  • zang also modifies Yogācāra’s three natures. He gives two aspects to each nature, allowing him to say that Yogācāra and Madhyamaka each recognize something true but emphasize different aspects.
  • e result is something like:
  • things conventionally appear;
  • they arise dependently;
  • they are empty of self-nature;
  • suchness is not separate from their dependent arising;
  • therefore the conditioned and unconditioned are neither simply identical nor separable.
  • is is a genuine synthesis, but it is Huayan’s reinterpretation of Yogācāra, not merely classical Indian Yogācāra reproduced accurately. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])

5. One Mind, Buddha-nature and ālayavijñāna

  • e thread’s most important source is not strictly an Indian Yogācāra text. It is the enormously influential Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna.
  • describes One Mind with two aspects or gateways:
  • the aspect of suchness;
  • the aspect of arising and ceasing, or saṃsāra.
  • ese are not two separate substances. They are two ways in which the same reality is encountered:
  • without delusive discrimination;
  • through conditioned ignorance and karmic appearance.
  • e text became foundational for East Asian Buddhism, especially Huayan and Chan, although its traditional attribution to the Indian author Aśvaghoṣa is historically disputed and modern scholarship gives serious attention to its Chinese formation. ([OUP Academic][4])

The forum’s problematic formulation

  • e Reddit poster says Buddha-nature is:
“fully eternal and fully impermanent.”
  • at is too blunt.
  • more accurate formulation is:
Suchness is unchanging insofar as emptiness never becomes non-emptiness, while phenomena continuously change insofar as they arise dependently. These are two inseparable aspects, not one entity possessing contradictory properties in exactly the same respect.
  • zang describes suchness as having:
  • an unchanging aspect;
  • an aspect that accompanies change.
  • e samsaric aspect arises and ceases according to conditions. Huayan therefore uses an aspectual logic: what appears contradictory becomes intelligible when the predicates apply under different perspectives. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])
  • milarly, ālayavijñāna is not simply a pure eternal entity. In the Awakening of Faith framework, it names the conjunction of:
  • the unborn and unceasing;
  • the born and ceasing.
  • is the dynamic structure through which suchness and conditioned delusion coexist, not a permanent personal soul.

6. Is One Mind basically Brahman?

  • is is the hardest question.
  • ere is an undeniable resemblance:
  • one all-pervading reality;
  • phenomena inseparable from that reality;
  • positive language such as purity, eternity and bliss;
  • liberation through recognizing one’s true nature.
  • at is why phrases such as “transpersonal self” appear in some modern interpretations of Huayan. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])
  • t Huayan tries to block a Brahman-like substantialist interpretation in several ways.

One Mind is not an individual subject

  • is not a cosmic person thinking the universe into existence.

It is not separate from phenomena

  • ere is no pure substance behind the world that could remain what it is without its manifestations.

Its “oneness” is nondual, not numerical

  • ne Mind” does not mean one enormous object instead of many small objects. Numerical oneness already contrasts one with many. Huayan instead claims that one and many are mutually constitutive.

It is empty

  • en Buddha-nature cannot possess an isolated self-nature. Its universality consists precisely in not being bounded, private or self-subsistent.
  • the safest conclusion is:
Huayan comes unusually close to an Absolute-style metaphysics, but its Absolute is supposed to be empty, relational and non-separate from the conditioned world—not an independently existing substrate.
  • ether Huayan completely avoids reifying One Mind remains a real philosophical dispute. A strict Madhyamaka thinker may say Huayan has smuggled a foundation back into emptiness. A Huayan thinker replies that One Mind is not an entity beneath relations; it is the entire empty-relational reality viewed without fragmentation.

7. The “one is all, all is one” doctrine

  • is is stronger than ordinary causal interdependence.
  • iyan’s Ten Mysteries include claims that:
  • every phenomenon causes and results from all others;
  • every phenomenon reflects all others recursively;
  • each includes and is included within all others;
  • each retains its distinctness while being identical with the whole relational order;
  • past, present and future are mutually implicated;
  • purity and defilement coexist under different aspects;
  • every phenomenon manifests the complete teaching. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])
  • is is sometimes described as “holographic,” but the metaphor can mislead. Huayan does not claim that a grain of sand physically stores miniature copies of every galaxy.
  • ther:
To understand the grain completely would require understanding every condition that made it this grain—its material history, conceptual identity, relations, perceivers, ecosystem, causal past and possible functions.
  • s full identity therefore opens indefinitely into the whole cosmos.

8. How Huayan connects with other East Asian schools

Chan/Zen

  • ayan had a very substantial relationship with Chan. Chengguan incorporated Chan into his classification of teachings, while Zongmi was simultaneously a Huayan patriarch and a Chan patriarch. Zongmi used Huayan metaphysics to explain sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])
  • is produces a natural division of labour:
  • Huayan: explains the structure of reality.
  • Chan: directly realizes that structure in mind and conduct.
  • t “Huayan is the philosophy and Zen is the practice” is a useful simplification, not a universal historical rule.

Pure Land

  • e Avataṃsaka world is filled with immeasurable buddhas and buddha-fields, so it harmonizes readily with Pure Land cosmology and devotional practice. The Awakening of Faith also recommends recollection of the Buddha as an accessible path.
  • vertheless, saying Huayan is the primary philosophy behind all Pure Land Buddhism is too broad. Pure Land has its own Indian sūtras, commentarial traditions and doctrinal systems.

Tiantai

  • antai independently produced another great Chinese synthesis. Its threefold truth—emptiness, provisional existence and the middle—resembles Huayan’s attempt to affirm emptiness and phenomenal reality simultaneously.
  • rough contrast:
  • Tiantai: every single moment of experience contains all realms and all possibilities.
  • Huayan: every phenomenon mutually contains and determines every other phenomenon.

Tathāgatagarbha traditions

  • ayan gives one of the most systematic East Asian expressions to original enlightenment and Buddha-nature. But it goes beyond merely saying that everyone can awaken. Buddha-nature becomes the suchness present throughout the entire dharma-realm.

9. What the Reddit discussion got right—and wrong

Strong points

  • e forum correctly recognized that:
  • Huayan unites emptiness, mind-only language and Buddha-nature.
  • It is not satisfied with a merely latent “potential” interpretation of Buddha-nature.
  • Indra’s net expresses more than simple causal interaction.
  • the Dilun and Shelun debates helped prepare Huayan.
  • Huayan differs strongly from Xuanzang’s Faxiang system.
  • One Mind is metaphysically suggestive but must not be treated casually as an ordinary self.
  • Buddhist philosophy cannot be separated completely from liberation and practice.

Points needing correction

“All phenomena stem from ālayavijñāna”

  • o simple. In classical Yogācāra the ālaya is a conditioned continuity carrying karmic seeds. In Huayan, ultimate language shifts toward tathāgatagarbha, suchness and One Mind.

“Tathāgatagarbha transforms into objects”

  • is sounds like a substance undergoing material transformation. Better:
Conditioned phenomena are the dynamic, dependently arisen aspect of the same empty reality whose true nature is suchness.

“Buddha-nature is simultaneously permanent and impermanent”

  • ly under different aspects. Huayan does not need to assert a flat contradiction.

“Huayan perfectly reconciles all Mahāyāna schools”

  • reconciles them according to Huayan’s own categories. Classical Madhyamaka or Faxiang Yogācāra need not accept Huayan’s interpretation of them.

“Huayan is the philosophy behind all East Asian Buddhism”

  • was immensely influential, especially on Chan, Korean Hwaeom/Seon and Japanese Kegon, but East Asian Buddhism also contains independent Tiantai, Pure Land, esoteric, Vinaya and other philosophical structures.

10. Best sources and reading order

Start here

  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: “Huayan Buddhism.”
  • e clearest free technical overview, covering Dushun, Zhiyan, Fazang, Chengguan, Zongmi, the four dharma-realms, One Mind and the three natures. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy][1])
  • Francis H. Cook — Hua-yen Buddhism: The Jewel Net of Indra.
  • obably the best short conceptual introduction. It explains interpenetration and Fazang without requiring a huge background in Chinese Buddhism. ([Penn State University Press][5])
  • Thomas Cleary — Entry Into the Inconceivable.
  • rticularly useful because it combines an introduction with translations of foundational Huayan writings, including materials associated with Dushun, Zhiyan, Fazang and Chengguan. ([UH Press][6])

Then read the doctrinal sources

  • Fazang — Treatise on the Doctrinal Distinctions of the Huayan One Vehicle.
  • is is the systematic source for Huayan’s classification of teachings, three natures and perfect teaching. A modern BDK English translation is available. ([BDK America][7])
  • The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna.
  • r One Mind, two aspects, original enlightenment, suchness and ālayavijñāna. The recent Jorgensen, Lusthaus, Makeham and Strange translation is the academically strongest option; Hakeda is shorter and more approachable. ([OUP Academic][4])
  • The Avataṃsaka Sūtra / Flower Ornament Scripture.
  • is is the imaginative scriptural universe behind the philosophy. Do not expect a linear philosophical treatise: it is a massive visionary text about bodhisattva practice, infinite worlds, Vairocana and mutual containment.

For serious scholarship

  • Imre Hamar, ed. — Reflecting Mirrors: Perspectives on Huayan Buddhism.
  • major scholarly collection covering Huayan history, doctrine, practice and its interpretation of Yogācāra. ([Google Books][8])
  • Imre Hamar — “The Huayan Understanding of One-Mind and Buddhist Practice.”
  • pecially relevant to the Reddit discussion because it directly explains how Huayan inherited Dilun/Shelun Yogācāra and interpreted the Awakening of Faith.
  • Peter N. Gregory — Tsung-mi and the Sinification of Buddhism.
  • st for Huayan’s relationship with Chan, original enlightenment and Chinese intellectual history. ([Google Books][9])

My verdict

  • e Reddit poster grasped Huayan’s overall beauty but presented it too much like an emanation system:
Buddha-nature → ālayavijñāna → individual objects.
  • ayan is better represented as a nondual relational circuit:
**Suchness is empty and therefore manifests through conditions.
Conditions are empty and therefore never depart from suchness.
Every conditioned phenomenon arises through the total field.
Therefore the one is present in the many, and the many constitute the one.**
  • is probably the most ambitious attempt in Buddhist philosophy to show not merely that everything is empty, but why emptiness makes possible an infinitely rich universe in which every particular matters.
